    Case Study 2 — Whole-scalp spectral analysis of resting-state EEG (R)¶

    This is the R implementation of Case Study 2. It implements the analysis described in Section 4.2 of the companion paper. The same analysis is also available as Python code.

    The research question is:

    Does the spectral profile of resting-state EEG relate to global cognitive functioning, without restricting the analysis in advance to a specific frequency band or region?

    Where Case Study 1 reduces the EEG signal to four theory-driven scalar features, this case study keeps the full power spectral density (PSD, 1–40 Hz, every channel) and asks broadly where — across the whole scalp and spectrum — resting EEG power relates to global cognition (MoCA), motivated by a well-established clinical observation: right-hemisphere stroke is frequently accompanied by pathological EEG slowing (more delta/theta power over the affected region) that tracks the severity of impairment (Finnigan & Van Putten, 2013).

    A note on the data¶

    • The EEG spectra used here are real, anonymised recordings.
    • The neuropsychological table (age, sex, CRIq, MoCA) is synthetic, as in Case Study 1.
    • Because the two do not come from the same assessment, the moca column was deliberately linked to a real, montage-based property of each EEG recording — see the notice at the top of data/generate_datasets.ipynb for the full disclosure. The resulting brain–behaviour association should not be read as a real clinical finding; it exists so this case study has something real to recover.

    Pipeline¶

    1. Data Wrangling — load & align, inspect, missing data, log-power distributions, covariate strategy
    2. Analysis — descriptive stats, a Case-Study-1-style baseline model, mass-univariate partial correlation, cluster-based permutation (primary whole-spectrum test + a pre-registered secondary/confirmatory test)
    3. Export — figures and tables (CSV + Excel)
    4. Strengths and limitations

    The Python version uses mne for electrode positions, spatial adjacency, and topographic plots. R has no equivalent package, so this instead reads three small, plain-CSV files — channel positions, channel adjacency, and the scalp outline — pre-exported from the real montage by data/EEG/PSD/compute_montage_assets.ipynb. Everything downstream (the statistics, the cluster test, the topomap interpolation) is plain R.

    How this code is built¶

    Like almost any real analysis, this notebook combines two things:

    1. Functions from established packages - the tidyverse (readr, dplyr, tidyr, purrr, stringr, ggplot2) to read, reshape and plot the data, broom to turn models into tables, Matrix, MASS and igraph for the linear algebra and graph steps, patchwork to combine plots, openxlsx for Excel export and cli for readable messages.
    2. A few custom functions for what no package we use here covers: a reader for NumPy's .npy files, the cluster-based permutation test, and the topographic map. In Python, numpy reads .npy files and mne draws the topomaps (the cluster test is a short custom function there too); R has packages for parts of this as well (e.g. reticulate, permuco, eegUtils), but to keep the dependencies light we use small helpers instead. They live in the R/ folder next to this notebook and are loaded in Setup, just as you would load a small package of your own
      • so the notebook itself reads as the analysis, step by step.

    The custom functions are hidden by default, but they are not a black box: wherever one is first used, a collapsed cell lets you print its source code (or simply open the file in R/).

    ⚠️ Caution - the custom functions in R/ (the .npy reader, the cluster-based permutation test and the topographic map) are minimal, didactic implementations, written only so this tutorial runs in R without extra dependencies. They are not extensively tested, and they are not a validated or published implementation of cluster-based permutation testing. For real analyses use established, peer-reviewed tools - MNE-Python, FieldTrip, or R packages such as permuco and eegUtils.

    Load the packages we use throughout the analysis, then our own helper functions from the R/ folder.

    1. Data Wrangling¶

    1.1 Load data¶

    The EEG spectra are stored as a [subjects x channels x frequencies] array, linked to the neuropsychological table by subject_id. Unlike Case Study 1's CSV files, this is too large for a spreadsheet — it comes as three companion files (the array, the channel names, the frequency axis), saved by Python's numpy.save. To keep the dependencies light, we read the (simple, documented) binary format with a small helper, read_npy(), from our R/ folder - the alternative would be calling numpy itself from R, through the reticulate package.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    psd_log     <- read_npy(file.path(PSD_DIR, "psd_log_matrix_full.npy"))  # [subjects x channels x freqs]
freqs       <- read_npy(file.path(PSD_DIR, "freq_axis.npy"))
ch_names    <- read_lines(file.path(PSD_DIR, "channel_names.txt"), skip_empty_rows = TRUE)
subject_ids <- read_lines(file.path(PSD_DIR, "subject_ids_full.txt"), skip_empty_rows = TRUE)

npsy <- read_csv(NPSY_CSV, show_col_types = FALSE)
erp  <- read_csv(ERP_CSV, show_col_types = FALSE)

n_subj <- dim(psd_log)[1]; n_ch <- dim(psd_log)[2]; n_freq <- dim(psd_log)[3]
cli_alert_info("PSD: {n_subj} subjects x {n_ch} channels x {n_freq} frequency bins ({fmt(min(freqs))}-{fmt(max(freqs))} Hz)")
glimpse(npsy)

# Strict alignment check: the PSD array and the NPSY table must refer to
# the same participants, in the same order (Section 4.2.2 of the paper
# flags this explicitly as a common failure point).
stopifnot(nrow(npsy) == n_subj, all(npsy$subject_id == subject_ids))
cli_alert_success("Subject alignment OK.")

    inspect
    Copied! 
    # Want to see how it works? Printing a function shows its source code.
print(read_npy)
    # Want to see how it works? Printing a function shows its source code. print(read_npy)
    function(path) {
  con <- file(path, "rb")
  on.exit(close(con))
  magic <- readBin(con, "raw", n = 6)
  stopifnot(rawToChar(magic[2:6]) == "NUMPY")
  major <- readBin(con, "integer", n = 1, size = 1, signed = FALSE)
  readBin(con, "integer", n = 1, size = 1, signed = FALSE)  # minor version, unused
  header_len <- if (major == 1) {
    readBin(con, "integer", n = 1, size = 2, signed = FALSE, endian = "little")
  } else {
    readBin(con, "integer", n = 1, size = 4, endian = "little")
  }
  header <- rawToChar(readBin(con, "raw", n = header_len))
  stopifnot(!grepl("'fortran_order':\\s*True", header))  # we only handle C order

  shape_str <- regmatches(header, regexpr("(?<=\'shape\':\\s\\()[^)]*", header, perl = TRUE))
  shape <- as.integer(trimws(strsplit(shape_str, ",")[[1]]))
  shape <- shape[!is.na(shape)]
  descr <- regmatches(header, regexpr("(?<=\'descr\':\\s\')[^\']+", header, perl = TRUE))
  size <- if (grepl("f8", descr)) 8 else 4

  vals <- readBin(con, "double", n = prod(shape), size = size, endian = "little")
  if (length(shape) == 1) return(vals)
  # row-major data into a column-major R array: fill with reversed
  # dims, then transpose the axis order back
  aperm(array(vals, dim = rev(shape)), rev(seq_along(shape)))
}

    1.2 Missing data and outliers¶

    As in Case Study 1 (see its Sections 1.3-1.6 for the full walk-through), a few participants have missing or implausible values. Since this is the same dataset, we exclude the same subjects here before any further inspection.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    subj_to_exclude <- c("sub-016", "sub-019", "sub-024", "sub-036", "sub-044")

# Missing values per column of the neuropsychological table
npsy %>% summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x))))

# Tables are filtered by subject_id; the PSD array (same subject order, as
# checked above) with a logical index
keep <- !(subject_ids %in% subj_to_exclude)
npsy <- npsy %>% filter(!subject_id %in% subj_to_exclude)
erp  <- erp %>% filter(!subject_id %in% subj_to_exclude)
psd_log <- psd_log[keep, , ]
subject_ids <- subject_ids[keep]
n_subj <- dim(psd_log)[1]

stopifnot(all(npsy$subject_id == subject_ids))
cli_alert_info("Excluded {length(subj_to_exclude)} participants - {n_subj} remaining.")

    1.3 Initial inspection¶

    A quick sanity check before anything else: does the grand-average spectrum look like a real EEG spectrum (1/f-like decay, no obvious line noise or flat channels)?

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    bands <- tribble(
  ~label,  ~lo, ~hi, ~color,
  "delta",   1,   4, "#e3f2fd",
  "theta",   4,   8, "#fff3e0",
  "alpha",   8,  13, "#e8f5e9",
  "beta",   13,  30, "#fce4ec",
  "gamma",  30,  40, "#f3e5f5"
)

spectrum <- tibble(
  freq = freqs,
  avg  = apply(psd_log, 3, mean),                    # grand average
  sd   = apply(apply(psd_log, c(1, 3), mean), 2, sd)  # SD across participants
)

fig_grandavg <- ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = bands, aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = label),
            alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = set_names(bands$color, bands$label), guide = "none") +
  geom_ribbon(data = spectrum, aes(freq, ymin = avg - sd, ymax = avg + sd), alpha = 0.2, fill = "#1f77b4") +
  geom_line(data = spectrum, aes(freq, avg), color = "#1f77b4", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = bands, aes(x = (lo + hi) / 2, y = max(spectrum$avg + spectrum$sd) * 0.97, label = label),
            vjust = 1, size = 3.2) +
  labs(x = "Frequency (Hz)", y = "Log power (a.u.)",
       title = str_glue("Grand-average log-power spectrum (n={n_subj}, mean ± SD across participants)"))
fig_grandavg

# Flag participants whose spectrum looks implausible (flat, or extreme overall level)
tibble(subject_id = subject_ids,
       level  = apply(psd_log, 1, mean),
       spread = apply(psd_log, 1, sd)) %>%
  mutate(flagged = abs(level - mean(level)) > 3 * sd(level) | spread < 1e-6) %>%
  summarise(mean_level = mean(level), min_level = min(level), max_level = max(level),
            n_flagged = sum(flagged))

    What do we see in the plot?

    A real EEG power spectrum is not flat: power is highest at low frequencies and decays roughly as 1/frequency (the "1/f" background), often with a small bump around 8–13 Hz (the alpha rhythm). A flat line, a spectrum with no decay, or a sharp spike at a single frequency (line noise, typically 50 or 60 Hz) would be a data-quality warning sign.

    1.4 Log-power distribution check¶

    The PSD array is already log-transformed (log-power is approximately normally distributed, whereas raw spectral power is strongly right- skewed — the same reason we log-transformed nothing extra here, unlike a raw-power pipeline would need to). With ~32,000 channel x frequency points, checking each one individually is neither possible nor useful; instead we check a handful of representative points.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    ci_mid   <- n_ch %/% 2
fi_delta <- which.min(abs(freqs - 2))
fi_alpha <- which.min(abs(freqs - 10))

point_label <- function(fi) str_c("Cz-like (central)\n", ch_names[ci_mid], " @ ", fmt(freqs[fi]), " Hz")

spot_check <- bind_rows(
  tibble(value = psd_log[, ci_mid, fi_delta], label = point_label(fi_delta)),
  tibble(value = psd_log[, ci_mid, fi_alpha], label = point_label(fi_alpha))
)

fig_dist <- ggplot(spot_check, aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "#1f77b4", alpha = 0.8, color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~label, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Log power", y = "Count")
fig_dist
    ci_mid <- n_ch %/% 2 fi_delta <- which.min(abs(freqs - 2)) fi_alpha <- which.min(abs(freqs - 10)) point_label <- function(fi) str_c("Cz-like (central)\n", ch_names[ci_mid], " @ ", fmt(freqs[fi]), " Hz") spot_check <- bind_rows( tibble(value = psd_log[, ci_mid, fi_delta], label = point_label(fi_delta)), tibble(value = psd_log[, ci_mid, fi_alpha], label = point_label(fi_alpha)) ) fig_dist <- ggplot(spot_check, aes(value)) + geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "#1f77b4", alpha = 0.8, color = "white") + facet_wrap(~label, scales = "free") + labs(x = "Log power", y = "Count") fig_dist

    What do we see in the plot?

    Both histograms are roughly bell-shaped and symmetric, not the strongly right-skewed shape raw (non-log) power would show — exactly the pattern that justifies working with log-power. The two points shown (a low and a high frequency, same central channel) are just a spot check; with ~32,000 channel x frequency points we can't inspect every one, but nothing here suggests the log transform failed to do its job.

    1.5 Covariate strategy¶

    Age and CRIq are covariates, as in Case Study 1. We use partial correlation: correlate log-power with MoCA after removing the linear effect of age and CRIq from both variables. This is simpler to explain than a two-step residualisation and gives the same result.

    2. Analysis¶

    2.1 Descriptive statistics¶

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    desc_vars <- c("age", "sex", "criq", "moca")

table1 <- npsy %>%
  select(all_of(desc_vars)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable") %>%
  drop_na(value) %>%
  mutate(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = desc_vars)) %>%
  group_by(Variable) %>%
  summarise(
    n     = n(),
    Value = str_c(fmt(mean(value), 2), " ± ", fmt(sd(value), 2)),
    Range = str_c("[", fmt(min(value), 2), ", ", fmt(max(value), 2), "]")
  ) %>%
  mutate(Variable = as.character(Variable))

    2.2 Baseline — a Case-Study-1-style model¶

    Before analysing the whole spectrum, we fit the kind of model Case Study 1 would use: a single, a-priori ERP feature (P300 amplitude) as a predictor of MoCA. This is deliberately naive here — P300 and resting- state PSD are conceptually different recordings (task-based vs. resting), so this model cannot detect the whole-scalp resting-state association we are looking for. It exists only to make the contrast concrete: a model that commits in advance to one feature can only find an association if it happens to live there.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    df_baseline <- inner_join(npsy, erp, by = "subject_id")
mod_baseline <- glm(moca ~ p300_amp + age + criq, data = df_baseline, family = gaussian())
summary(mod_baseline)
    df_baseline <- inner_join(npsy, erp, by = "subject_id") mod_baseline <- glm(moca ~ p300_amp + age + criq, data = df_baseline, family = gaussian()) summary(mod_baseline)

    2.3 Mass-univariate partial correlation¶

    We now use the real, full-resolution spectrum. At every channel x frequency point, we compute the partial correlation between log-power and MoCA, controlling for age and CRIq, and convert it to a t-statistic. This produces one map of 204 x 159 test statistics.

    # Want to see how it works? Printing a function shows its source code.
print(partial_corr_tmap)
    # Want to see how it works? Printing a function shows its source code. print(partial_corr_tmap)
    function(log_power, y, covariates) {
  n <- length(y)
  Z <- cbind(1, as.matrix(covariates))
  Z_pinv <- MASS::ginv(Z)
  resid_y <- y - Z %*% (Z_pinv %*% y)
  Y <- matrix(aperm(log_power, c(1, 3, 2)), nrow = n)
  resid_power <- Y - Z %*% (Z_pinv %*% Y)
  num <- as.vector(t(resid_y) %*% resid_power)
  den <- sqrt(sum(resid_y^2)) * sqrt(colSums(resid_power^2))
  r <- pmax(pmin(num / den, 0.999999), -0.999999)
  df <- n - ncol(Z) - 1   # n - intercept - covariates - y
  r * sqrt(df / (1 - r^2))
}
<bytecode: 0x16ee48c78>

    What do we see in the plot?

    Each pixel is one channel x frequency combination; colour is the t-value of its partial correlation with MoCA (red = positive, blue = negative). This map on its own is not trustworthy: with ~32,000 simultaneous tests, a conventional p<0.05 threshold would flag over 1,600 points purely by chance. We need a correction that accounts for how many tests we ran and respects the fact that neighbouring points are not independent — which is exactly what cluster-based permutation testing does (next section).

    2.4 Cluster-based permutation test¶

    The idea, in plain terms: instead of correcting each point in isolation, we group neighbouring suprathreshold points into clusters (a point is a neighbour of another if they are adjacent channels at the same frequency, or the same channel at adjacent frequency bins), sum the t-values within each cluster, and ask: if MoCA were randomly shuffled across participants (so any true association is destroyed), how often would a cluster this large arise purely by chance? We estimate that by actually shuffling MoCA thousands of times and recomputing the largest cluster each time — this is the permutation null distribution. A cluster's p-value is simply the fraction of shuffles that produced a cluster at least as extreme as the one we observed.

    Spatial adjacency comes from the real 3D positions of the EGI-256 montage, pre-exported by compute_montage_assets.ipynb; spectral adjacency links consecutive frequency bins (Maris & Oostenveld, 2007).

    We run two, pre-planned analyses:

    • Primary — the whole spectrum (1–40 Hz), every channel, no a priori restriction. This is the test the paper's framing is built around: it can find an effect anywhere, at the cost of a large multiple- comparisons penalty.
    • Secondary / confirmatory — restricted a priori to the region the clinical literature actually predicts (right hemisphere, delta/theta, 1–8 Hz). Restricting the search space before looking at the data is standard practice when there is a specific hypothesis, and it recovers power the whole-spectrum test gives up. We report both, rather than only the one that "worked", precisely to avoid the circular reasoning Case Study 1 warned about (Section 2.3 there): the secondary result is only informative because it was planned, not because we went looking for whichever restriction happened to be significant.

    ⚠️ Caution - the cluster-based permutation functions used here (cluster_permutation_test() and its helpers, in R/cluster_permutation.R) are a minimal, didactic implementation, written only so this tutorial runs in R without extra dependencies. They are not extensively tested and are not a validated or published implementation of the method. For real analyses use established, peer-reviewed tools - MNE-Python (mne.stats), FieldTrip, or the R package permuco.

    function(edges, ch_names) {
  ch_index <- set_names(seq_along(ch_names), ch_names)
  i1 <- ch_index[edges$ch1]
  i2 <- ch_index[edges$ch2]
  n <- length(ch_names)
  sparseMatrix(i = c(i1, i2), j = c(i2, i1), x = 1, dims = c(n, n))
}

    function(spatial_adj, n_freq) {
  n_ch <- nrow(spatial_adj)
  kronecker(spatial_adj, Diagonal(n_freq)) + kronecker(Diagonal(n_ch), freq_chain_adjacency(n_freq))

    function(log_power, y, covariates, adjacency,
                                     t_thresh = 2.028, n_perm = 2000, seed = 1) {
  n_ch <- dim(log_power)[2]
  n_freq <- dim(log_power)[3]
  set.seed(seed)
  t_obs <- partial_corr_tmap(log_power, y, covariates)
  obs_clusters <- find_clusters(t_obs, t_thresh, adjacency)
  obs_clusters <- obs_clusters[order(-abs(sapply(obs_clusters, function(c) c$mass)))]
  n <- length(y)
  null_max <- numeric(n_perm)
  for (i in seq_len(n_perm)) {
    shuffled <- sample(n)
    t_perm <- partial_corr_tmap(log_power, y[shuffled], covariates)
    cl <- find_clusters(t_perm, t_thresh, adjacency)
    null_max[i] <- if (length(cl) == 0) 0 else max(abs(sapply(cl, function(c) c$mass)))
  }
  results <- list()
  top <- obs_clusters[seq_len(min(5, length(obs_clusters)))]
  for (c in top) {
    p <- mean(null_max >= abs(c$mass))
    results[[length(results) + 1]] <- list(members = c$members, mass = c$mass, p_cluster = p)
  }
  list(clusters = results, t_obs = flat_to_map(t_obs, n_ch, n_freq))
}
<bytecode: 0x1329ec800>

    function(t_flat, t_thresh, adjacency) {
  clusters <- list()
  for (sign in c(1, -1)) {
    supra <- which((t_flat * sign) > t_thresh)
    if (length(supra) == 0) next
    # build the suprathreshold subgraph straight from the sparse
    # adjacency's own (i, j) triplets, without ever densifying it
    sub_adj <- as(adjacency[supra, supra], "TsparseMatrix")
    el <- cbind(sub_adj@i + 1L, sub_adj@j + 1L)
    el <- el[el[, 1] < el[, 2], , drop = FALSE]
    g <- igraph::make_empty_graph(n = length(supra), directed = FALSE)
    if (nrow(el) > 0) g <- igraph::add_edges(g, as.vector(t(el)))
    comp <- igraph::components(g)
    for (k in seq_len(comp$no)) {
      members <- supra[comp$membership == k]
      clusters[[length(clusters) + 1]] <- list(members = members, mass = sum(t_flat[members]))
    }
  }
  clusters
}
<bytecode: 0x10dfc9760>

    function(clusters, freqs, w_right, ch_index_map, label) {
  clusters %>%
    imap(function(cl, rank) {
      idx <- arrayInd(cl$members, .dim = c(length(freqs), length(ch_index_map)))
      fi <- idx[, 1]
      ci <- idx[, 2]
      tibble(
        Analysis        = label,
        `Cluster rank`  = rank,
        `Cluster mass`  = cl$mass,
        `N points`      = length(cl$members),
        `Freq min (Hz)` = min(freqs[fi]),
        `Freq max (Hz)` = max(freqs[fi]),
        `Mean w_right`  = mean(w_right[ch_index_map[unique(ci)]]),
        p_cluster       = cl$p_cluster
      )
    }) %>%
    list_rbind()
}

    Reading the result honestly: the primary, whole-spectrum test is not expected to survive correction at n=40 — this mirrors the paper's own caveat that cluster-based permutation is relatively underpowered at this sample size, so only fairly marked associations are likely to survive. The secondary, pre-registered test recovers a significant cluster, consistent with the hypothesised right-hemisphere, low-frequency pattern.

    2.5 Where is the effect? (topography of the significant cluster)¶

    For the significant cluster from the secondary analysis, we plot a topographic map of the (partial-correlation) t-values, averaged over the cluster's frequency range, with the cluster's channels highlighted.

    The scalp outline and 2D electrode positions below are the same ones mne.viz.plot_topomap uses for this montage, pre-exported (so this never has to invent its own projection); the colour surface itself is a simple, local loess smoother over the real channel values. Rather than adding a full EEG package for a single plot, we use a small helper, topomap_plot(), from our R/ folder (the eegUtils package offers a full-featured alternative).

print(topomap_plot)
    # Want to see how it works? Printing a function shows its source code. print(topomap_plot)
    function(values, montage, mask = NULL, title = "", vlim = NULL, grid_n = 100) {
  r_max <- montage$clip_radius
  grid <- expand_grid(x2d = seq(-r_max, r_max, length.out = grid_n),
                      y2d = seq(-r_max, r_max, length.out = grid_n))
  fit <- loess(value ~ x2d * y2d,
               data = tibble(x2d = montage$pos_2d$x2d, y2d = montage$pos_2d$y2d, value = values),
               degree = 2, span = 0.35, control = loess.control(surface = "direct"))
  grid <- grid %>%
    mutate(pred = as.vector(predict(fit, newdata = grid))) %>%
    filter(sqrt(x2d^2 + y2d^2) <= r_max)   # keep only the inside of the head

  if (is.null(vlim)) {
    lim <- max(abs(values), na.rm = TRUE)
    vlim <- c(-lim, lim)
  }

  head_outline <- montage$outline %>%
    filter(part %in% c("head", "nose", "ear_left", "ear_right"))

  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_raster(data = grid, aes(x2d, y2d, fill = pred)) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0,
                         limits = vlim, oob = scales::squish, na.value = NA, name = "t-value") +
    geom_path(data = head_outline, aes(x, y, group = part), color = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
    coord_fixed() +
    theme_void() +
    ggtitle(title)

  if (!is.null(mask) && any(mask)) {
    p <- p + geom_point(data = montage$pos_2d[mask, ], aes(x2d, y2d),
                        shape = 16, size = 1.2, color = "black")
  }
  p
}

    What do we see in the plot?

    A clear right-lateralised, negative (blue) region over the posterior-right scalp, with the significant cluster's channels marked as black dots inside it — exactly the hemisphere and sign (lower MoCA, higher delta/theta power) the clinical hypothesis predicted. The left hemisphere, shown with real data too, is comparatively flat: the effect isn't a generic "more power is worse" pattern, it's localised to the predicted side.

    2.6 Illustrative check: PSD by MoCA level¶

    Purely for illustration (not a separate statistical test), we split participants by a median MoCA split and plot the average spectrum at the cluster's channels for each group.

    What do we see in the plot?

    The lower-MoCA group (red) sits above the higher-MoCA group (blue) across most of the spectrum, and the gap is most visible within the shaded significant-cluster range (1–8 Hz) — consistent with the cluster test's finding of more low-frequency power in participants with poorer cognition. This is a median split shown only for intuition, not a second statistical test: the real evidence is the cluster-permutation result above.

    2.7 Exploratory: which canonical band drives the effect?¶

    The secondary analysis above pools delta and theta (1–8 Hz) into a single test. It is natural to ask whether the effect is really carried by both, or mainly by one of them — and whether it is genuinely absent in alpha/beta/gamma, as the clinical hypothesis would predict.

    This is an exploratory, supplementary analysis, not a substitute for the pre-registered primary/secondary tests above. We repeat the same cluster-permutation procedure (same right-hemisphere ROI, same threshold) separately for each of the five canonical bands. Because this means testing five hypotheses instead of one, we apply a Bonferroni correction across bands (multiply each band's p-value by 5, capped at 1) — exactly the kind of correction Case Study 1 discussed for multiple outcomes, applied here to multiple frequency bands instead.

    In [22]:
    Copied! 
    CANONICAL_BANDS <- list(delta = c(1, 4), theta = c(4, 8), alpha = c(8, 13),
                        beta = c(13, 30), gamma = c(30, 40))

band_results <- imap(CANONICAL_BANDS, function(limits, band) {
  band_freq_idx <- which(freqs >= limits[1] & freqs < limits[2])
  band_adjacency <- combine_adjacency(roi_spatial_adjacency, length(band_freq_idx))
  res <- cluster_permutation_test(psd_log[, right_idx, band_freq_idx], moca, covariates, band_adjacency,
                                  t_thresh = T_THRESH, n_perm = N_PERM, seed = 1)
  # the largest cluster (or an empty one, if nothing crossed the threshold)
  top <- if (length(res$clusters) > 0) res$clusters[[1]] else list(mass = 0, members = integer(0), p_cluster = 1)
  list(freq_range = limits, freq_idx = band_freq_idx, top = top,
       p_bonferroni = min(top$p_cluster * length(CANONICAL_BANDS), 1))
})

table4_bands <- band_results %>%
  imap(function(res, band) {
    tibble(
      Band                   = band,
      `Freq min (Hz)`        = res$freq_range[1],
      `Freq max (Hz)`        = res$freq_range[2],
      `Cluster mass`         = res$top$mass,
      `N points`             = length(res$top$members),
      p_raw                  = res$top$p_cluster,
      `p_bonferroni (x5)`    = res$p_bonferroni,
      `Significant (p<0.05)` = res$p_bonferroni < 0.05
    )
  }) %>%
  list_rbind()
table4_bands

    Copied! 
    band_panels <- imap(band_results, function(res, band) {
  in_band <- freqs >= res$freq_range[1] & freqs < res$freq_range[2]
  t_avg_band <- rowMeans(t_obs_primary[, in_band, drop = FALSE])

  significant <- res$p_bonferroni < 0.05
  mask <- rep(FALSE, n_ch)
  if (significant) {
    idx <- arrayInd(res$top$members, .dim = c(length(res$freq_idx), n_ch_roi))
    mask[right_idx[unique(idx[, 2])]] <- TRUE
  }

  topomap_plot(
    t_avg_band, montage, mask = mask, vlim = c(-3, 3),
    title = str_glue("{band} ({res$freq_range[1]}-{res$freq_range[2]} Hz)\n",
                     "p={fmt(res$p_bonferroni, 3)} ({if (significant) 'significant' else 'n.s.'})")
  )
})

fig_bands <- wrap_plots(band_panels, nrow = 1) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(title = "Exploratory: right-hemisphere cluster test per canonical band\n(marked channels = significant cluster, Bonferroni-corrected across 5 bands)") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
fig_bands
    band_panels <- imap(band_results, function(res, band) { in_band <- freqs >= res$freq_range[1] & freqs < res$freq_range[2] t_avg_band <- rowMeans(t_obs_primary[, in_band, drop = FALSE]) significant <- res$p_bonferroni < 0.05 mask <- rep(FALSE, n_ch) if (significant) { idx <- arrayInd(res$top$members, .dim = c(length(res$freq_idx), n_ch_roi)) mask[right_idx[unique(idx[, 2])]] <- TRUE } topomap_plot( t_avg_band, montage, mask = mask, vlim = c(-3, 3), title = str_glue("{band} ({res$freq_range[1]}-{res$freq_range[2]} Hz)\n", "p={fmt(res$p_bonferroni, 3)} ({if (significant) 'significant' else 'n.s.'})") ) }) fig_bands <- wrap_plots(band_panels, nrow = 1) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") + plot_annotation(title = "Exploratory: right-hemisphere cluster test per canonical band\n(marked channels = significant cluster, Bonferroni-corrected across 5 bands)") & theme(legend.position = "bottom") fig_bands

    What do we see in the plots?

    Each panel is one canonical band, coloured by the same t-value scale; a panel's channels would be marked if that band's cluster survived correction for having tested five bands. This is a noticeably messier picture than a clean "low frequencies yes, high frequencies no" split: none of the five individual bands survives Bonferroni correction (theta comes closest, at a raw p≈0.03 that is no longer below 0.05 once multiplied by 5), even though several bands show the same right-lateralised, negative direction as the pre-registered secondary test above.

    This is a more informative result than a clean split would have been, for two reasons. First, it is a direct, concrete illustration of why multiple-comparison correction matters: taken on its own, theta's raw p-value would look like a finding — it only stops looking like one once we account for having tested five bands instead of pre-committing to one. Second, it shows why the secondary analysis pooled delta and theta together rather than testing them separately: combining adjacent frequency bins into one wider band gives the cluster more points to draw statistical mass from, which is exactly what recovers the significant result there. Splitting the spectrum into ever-narrower slices trades away the power that made the pooled test work in the first place — the same lesson Case Study 1 taught about predictors, now shown for frequency bands.

    4. Strengths and limitations of this approach (Section 4.2.3)¶

    Strengths:

    • No a priori commitment to a specific band or region — able to recover a distributed, low-frequency, right-hemisphere pattern that no single ERP feature (Case Study 1) would capture (Section 2.2 above)
    • Respects the real spatial and spectral dependency structure of the signal, unlike testing every point independently

    Limitations:

    • Computationally heavier than the GLM-based approach of Case Study 1
    • Statistically demanding: with around forty participants, cluster-based permutation is relatively underpowered, so only fairly marked associations are likely to survive — the whole-spectrum (primary) test in Section 2.4 illustrates this directly
    • A significant secondary result depends on having pre-registered the restricted region before looking at the data; restricting only after seeing what "worked" would be the same circular reasoning Case Study 1 warned against, just at the level of search space instead of predictor selection

    For a full discussion, see Section 4.2 of the companion paper, and Section 5.1 on general caveats (multiple comparisons, and not equating analytical complexity with validity).
